MRCT regional consistency via subgroup identification

A harmed subgroup found outside the region and applied inside it

This article reproduces, with every call visible, the regional-consistency strategy of the mrct-consistency technical report: a multiregional trial is positive overall, one region looks unfavourable, and a subgroup identified by forestsearch() on the patients outside the region is applied inside it.

NoteInstalling forestsearch

The CRAN release of forestsearch (0.4.0) does not yet contain the functions this article uses, so the last step below installs the development version from GitHub. Run the steps in a fresh R session.

# 1. a reliable CRAN mirror, and a longer download limit than R's default of 60 seconds
options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org"), timeout = 600)

# 2. the CRAN release, which installs every package forestsearch needs
install.packages("forestsearch")

# 3. two packages forestsearch only suggests, which this article uses (speff2trial for the
#    ACTG 175 data, latentcor for the copula expansion), and remotes for the next step
install.packages(c("speff2trial", "latentcor", "remotes"))

# 4. the development version from GitHub; upgrade = "never" leaves the packages above as they are
remotes::install_github("larry-leon/forestsearch", upgrade = "never")
packageVersion("forestsearch")

Step 4 downloads the whole forestsearch repository, several gigabytes, and builds only the package from it, so it takes several minutes; the longer download limit of step 1 is what lets it finish. If a step asks whether to install packages from sources, answer no. The chunk below stops with a message naming anything that is missing, before any computation starts.

Rendering needs the Quarto command-line tools and about five minutes. To render the article outside any working copy of the repository, fetch only the article and its data folder (a few megabytes) into a scratch folder and render it there:

git clone --depth 1 --filter=blob:none --sparse https://github.com/larry-leon/forestsearch.git ~/scratch/fs-article
cd ~/scratch/fs-article && git sparse-checkout set vignettes/articles

The rendered mrct-consistency.html is written beside the .qmd. Delete the scratch folder when done.

1 Overview: the question and the design

1.1 The trigger and the question

A global trial meets its primary endpoint: the upper 95% limit of the all-patient Cox hazard ratio is below 1.0 (ITT ub < 1.0). One region, about a fifth of the patients, has a Cox point estimate above 1.0 (region ITT > 1.0). The pair, in the same trial, is the trigger: the regional consistency failure as it presents in oncology multiregional trials. Region ITT > 1.0 describes a point estimate.

We consider two explanations for the trigger: the region differs in its treatment effect, or the trial contains a subgroup that is harmed, present in every region, and the region’s estimate is pulled up by it (with the region’s prognosis and the finite follow-up window shaping how far). The question is whether a subgroup identified on the non-region patients can account for the regional result: if removing it from the region leaves a Cox estimate below 1.0, the regional result is compatible with a trial-wide subgroup and does not by itself point to a region-specific effect. The strategy is signal generation, not confirmation.

ImportantThe region in this article

ACTG 175 was not a multiregional trial and has no region variable. The region used here is hypothetical: about 20% of patients, planted in a simulated population by a logistic model (Section 4.1). The way a region enters an analysis differs between real data and simulation:

  • In a real analysis the region is an observed column of the trial data and nothing about it is modelled. The trial is split into the region’s patients and the rest; the identifier runs on the rest; the declared rule is applied to the region.
  • In simulation the region has to be generated together with the patients. Here, with no observed region, it is planted by a model. With a trial that has an observed region, the observed region is carried into the data-generating mechanism instead (Section 3).

Replicate 5 of S2, the case study, is one simulated trial. From the point at which its data are read (Section 2), it is analysed exactly as a real trial would be.

1.2 The pipeline, for one trial

  1. Fit the all-patient Cox model of treatment. If ITT ub \(\ge\) 1.0, stop: the trial is not positive.
  2. Fit the region’s Cox model. If region ITT \(\le\) 1.0, stop: the trigger is not reached.
  3. Run the identifier, forestsearch(), on the non-region patients. It declares a subgroup \(\hat H\), a rule in at most two baseline covariates, or nothing.
  4. Apply \(\hat H\) inside the region; \(\hat G\) = region minus \(\hat H\). Fit the region’s Cox model on \(\hat G\).
  5. Record whether region(\(\hat G\)) < 1.0; the trigger together with region(\(\hat G\)) < 1.0 is joint. Record, as the oracle, whether region(\(G^*\)) < 1.0, with \(G^*\) = region minus the true harmed subgroup \(H^*\). In simulation, also record the sensitivity and specificity of \(\hat H\) against \(H^*\) on both sides.

\(\hat H\) is learned on the non-region patients only and applied to the region, whose outcomes the identifier never sees: the region is a held-out test set, and its Cox fits on the whole region and on \(\hat G\) are ordinary Wald fits on sets defined by a fixed rule. The non-region estimate inside \(\hat H\) is selected; Section 2.3 bounds it by multiplier resampling.

Labels used throughout.
Label Meaning
trigger ITT ub < 1.0 and region ITT > 1.0, in the same trial
\(H^*\) the true harmed subgroup, here CD4 \(\le\) 230 cells/mm³
\(\hat H\) the subgroup the identifier declares on the non-region patients
\(\hat G\), \(G^*\) region minus \(\hat H\); region minus \(H^*\) (the oracle)
\(\hat H^c\) the non-region complement of \(\hat H\): non-region patients not in \(\hat H\) (not \(\hat G\))
joint the trigger and region(\(\hat G\)) < 1.0; with \(G^*\) in place of \(\hat G\), the oracle joint
Sens / Spec of \(\hat H\) against \(H^*\), on the non-region patients and in the region
AHR average hazard ratio of a set: \(\exp\) of its patients’ mean log hazard ratio
CDE controlled direct effect: the ratio of the set’s mean hazards under the two arms
margHR(40), margHR(\(\infty\)) the marginal hazard ratio: the limit of the set’s two-sample Cox estimate at the 40-month analysis, and with no censoring
TipHow to use this article

Section 2 is the analysis of one trial, replicate 5 of S2, read from a shipped dataset and taken from the first Cox fit to the bounds on the declared subgroup. With your own trial, follow the same steps with your data frame and your column names; nothing in that section depends on how the trial arose. Section 3 shows how to set up simulations around your trial, treating replicate 5 as if it were yours, with its region observed. Section 4.1 onward is the report’s own simulation design, which generated replicate 5, and its results.

2 The case study: replicate 5 of S2

This section analyses one trial from its data to its bounds. The trial is replicate 5 of S2, shipped as rep5_trial.csv (one row per patient; its provenance is in PROVENANCE.md), and nothing below reads the simulation sections. The columns are the ones the analysis uses: the patient id, the time y_sim in months, the event indicator event_sim, the treatment treat_sim (1 = experimental), the region indicator z_region, the twelve baseline covariates the identifier is given (z_age to z_symptom, on their natural scales), and flag_harm, membership of \(H^*\). A real trial has no flag_harm; here it is used only for the region(\(G^*\)) row of step 4 and in Section 4.5.

Code 
trial <- rd("rep5_trial.csv")
covs <- c("z_age", "z_wtkg", "z_karnof", "z_preanti", "z_cd40", "z_cd80",
          "z_hemo", "z_homo", "z_drugs", "z_race", "z_gender", "z_symptom")
# the replicate's call seed, from the MR campaign's record of this trial
seed_rep5 <- rd("mr_field_S2_rep5.csv")$seed
stopifnot(length(seed_rep5) == 1, !anyDuplicated(trial$id),
          all(c("id", "y_sim", "event_sim", "treat_sim", "z_region", covs, "flag_harm") %in% names(trial)))
c(patients = nrow(trial), experimental = sum(trial$treat_sim == 1), events = sum(trial$event_sim),
  region = sum(trial$z_region == 1), non_region = sum(trial$z_region == 0), call_seed = seed_rep5)
    patients experimental       events       region   non_region    call_seed 
        1000          500          405          194          806    613800005

With your trial: read your data frame, and name its time, event, treatment (1 = experimental) and region (1 = in the region) columns and the baseline covariates the identifier may use.

2.1 Step 1: the all-patient Cox fit

Code 
fit_itt <- summary(coxph(Surv(y_sim, event_sim) ~ treat_sim, data = trial))
itt_ub <- fit_itt$conf.int[1, "upper .95"]
c(ITT_HR = fit_itt$conf.int[1, "exp(coef)"], lower = fit_itt$conf.int[1, "lower .95"], ITT_ub = itt_ub)
   ITT_HR     lower    ITT_ub 
0.8084137 0.6649320 0.9828564
Code 
stopifnot(itt_ub < 1)

The upper 95% limit is 0.983, below 1.0: the trial is positive. With your trial: your time, event and treatment columns in the formula; if ITT ub \(\ge\) 1.0 the pipeline stops here.

2.2 Step 2: the region’s Cox fit, and the trigger

Code 
reg <- trial$z_region == 1
fit_reg <- summary(coxph(Surv(y_sim, event_sim) ~ treat_sim, data = trial[reg, ]))
hr_reg <- fit_reg$conf.int[1, "exp(coef)"]
trigger <- itt_ub < 1 && hr_reg > 1
c(region_HR = hr_reg, lower = fit_reg$conf.int[1, "lower .95"], upper = fit_reg$conf.int[1, "upper .95"],
  region_events = sum(trial$event_sim[reg]), trigger = trigger)
    region_HR         lower         upper region_events       trigger 
    1.0364000     0.5558252     1.9324870    40.0000000     1.0000000
Code 
stopifnot(trigger)

The region’s estimate is 1.036, above 1.0, from 40 events: the trigger. With your trial: your region column in reg; if region ITT \(\le\) 1.0 the pipeline stops here.

2.3 Step 3: the identifier on the non-region patients, with post-selection inference

forestsearch() runs on the non-region patients, with the region’s patients passed as the test set (df.test) to which the declared rule is applied, with the campaign’s arguments: candidate cuts on the observed covariates with deciles for CD4, weight and prior ART, at most two factors, hazard-ratio threshold 0.90 for screening and 0.80 for consistency at probability 0.90, the largest consistent subgroup within an effect neighbourhood of 0.20 of the largest effect. Multiplier resampling (MR, mr_inference = TRUE) follows in the same call: 2,000 Poisson multiplier draws, the complement de-biased and given its own field (include_complement, field_complement), the field method at its default Monte Carlo sizes, the re-selections returned, and the replicate’s call seed. The call is the one mrct_case_study() makes (Section 4.4), written out; it runs under R’s default generator.

Code 
stopifnot(RNGkind()[1] == "Mersenne-Twister")
t_mr <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
fs <- forestsearch(
  df.analysis = trial[!reg, ], df.test = trial[reg, ],
  outcome.name = "y_sim", event.name = "event_sim", treat.name = "treat_sim", id.name = "id",
  confounders.name = covs, conf_force = character(0),
  conf.cont_jcuts = list(z_cd40 = 10, z_wtkg = 10, z_preanti = 10),
  use_grf = FALSE, use_lasso = FALSE, maxk = 2,
  hr.threshold = 0.90, hr.consistency = 0.80, pconsistency.threshold = 0.90,
  sg_focus = "hrMaxSG", effect_neighborhood = 0.20,
  mr_inference = TRUE,
  mr_inference_args = list(ci_method = "field", include_complement = TRUE, field_complement = TRUE,
                           draws = 2000, multiplier = "poisson", return_reselection = TRUE,
                           seed = seed_rep5),
  parallel_args = list(plan = "sequential"),
  show_candidate_summary = FALSE, details = FALSE, plot.sg = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
t_mr <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t_mr
mr <- fs$mr_inference
Hhat_def <- paste(fs$sg.harm, collapse = " & ")
stopifnot(!is.null(fs$sg.harm), mr$ci_method == "field", mr$settings$draws == 2000,
          mr$field$n_out_used == mr$field$R_out)
c(seconds = round(t_mr, 1), candidate_family = mr$n_family, n_Hhat = mr$n_selected,
  n_Hhat_complement = mr$complement$n)
          seconds  candidate_family            n_Hhat n_Hhat_complement 
             24.3            3003.0              73.0             733.0
Code 
Hhat_def
[1] "{z_cd40 <= 236} & !{z_preanti <= 196}"

\(\hat H\) is {z_cd40 <= 236} & !{z_preanti <= 196} (!{…} is the complement): CD4 \(\le\) 236 and prior ART over 196 days. The call took 24 seconds on one thread. With your trial: df.analysis and df.test are your non-region and region rows; your column names go in outcome.name, event.name, treat.name and id.name, your covariates in confounders.name, and those of your continuous covariates to be cut at deciles in conf.cont_jcuts; the other arguments are the identifier’s settings used throughout this article, and seed is yours.

2.4 Step 4: \(\hat H\) applied to the region; the four sets

Each set is analysed by the unweighted two-sample Cox fit of treatment, with the Wald 95% interval. \(\hat H\) is read for every patient from the identifier’s selected rule (get_dfpred()), checked against its classification of the analysis and test sets; \(\hat G\) is the region minus \(\hat H\). The region(\(G^*\)) row is here only because the trial is simulated (flag_harm).

Code 
in_Hhat <- get_dfpred(trial, sg.harm = fs$sg.harm, version = 2)$treat.recommend == 0
stopifnot(identical(in_Hhat, trial$id %in% c(fs$df.est$id[fs$df.est$treat.recommend == 0],
                                              fs$df.test$id[fs$df.test$treat.recommend == 0])))
cox_set <- function(d) {
  f <- summary(coxph(Surv(y_sim, event_sim) ~ treat_sim, data = d))
  ex <- d$treat_sim == 1
  data.frame(n = nrow(d), n_exp = sum(ex), n_ctl = sum(!ex),
             events_exp = sum(d$event_sim[ex]), events_ctl = sum(d$event_sim[!ex]),
             hr = f$conf.int[1, "exp(coef)"], lo = f$conf.int[1, "lower .95"], hi = f$conf.int[1, "upper .95"])
}
Hstar <- trial$flag_harm == 1                       # simulation only: H* is unknown in a real trial
set_idx <- list(itt_all = rep(TRUE, nrow(trial)), itt_region = reg,
                region_Gstar = reg & !Hstar, region_Ghat = reg & !in_Hhat)
four <- data.frame(set = names(set_idx), do.call(rbind, lapply(set_idx, function(i) cox_set(trial[i, ]))),
                   row.names = NULL)
stopifnot(near(four$hr[1:2], c(fit_itt$conf.int[1, "exp(coef)"], hr_reg), 1e-12))
set_label <- c(itt_all = "All patients, ITT", itt_region = "Region, ITT",
               region_Gstar = "Region minus H* (G*)", region_Ghat = "Region minus Ĥ (Ĝ)")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Set = set_label[four$set], n = four$n,
                        `experimental n / events` = sprintf("%d / %d", four$n_exp, four$events_exp),
                        `control n / events` = sprintf("%d / %d", four$n_ctl, four$events_ctl),
                        HR = f3(four$hr), `95% CI` = sprintf("%s, %s", f3(four$lo), f3(four$hi)),
                        check.names = FALSE),
             row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrr", caption = "Replicate 5 of S2: the four sets.")

Code 
par(op)

The trial is positive (ITT upper limit 0.983 < 1.0) and its region is above 1.0 (1.036, 40 events): the trigger. Applied in the region, \(\hat H\) removes 20 patients, and region(\(\hat G\)) is 0.844, below 1.0: the trial is joint. Every interval is wide: the regional sets have few events, so the move of the regional estimate from above 1 to below 1 is an explanation consistent with a trial-wide harmed subgroup, not confirmation of it. With your trial: get_dfpred() applies your \(\hat H\) to all your rows; drop the region(\(G^*\)) row, as \(H^*\) is unknown.

WarningWhat the move below 1.0 shows, and what it does not

Removing \(\hat H\) from the region and refitting the Cox model compares two different patient sets; it does not decompose the regional hazard ratio. The region’s estimate is not a weighted average of the estimates in \(\hat H\) and in \(\hat G\): removing patients changes the risk sets, the events and the censoring mixture, and each Cox estimate converges to the limit of its own set at the analysis time (Section 4.3), which can differ from that set’s AHR or CDE. A regional estimate that moves from above 1.0 to below 1.0 is therefore compatible with a trial-wide subgroup accounting for the regional result. It does not show that \(\hat H\) caused it, does not validate \(\hat H\) as a clinically actionable subgroup, and, read with the null cells (Section 5), can arise when there is no harmed subgroup at all.

2.5 Step 5: the Pareto frontier and the bounds

The Pareto frontier: the admitted candidates that no other candidate beats on both hazard ratio and size, with half-sample (split) 95% intervals from compute_frontier_cis() (1,000 random halvings per member) and the effect neighbourhood 0.20 shaded; \(\hat H\) is the selected member.

Code 
ci_front <- compute_frontier_cis(fs, n_splits = 1000L, seed = seed_rep5)
pf <- fs$grp.consistency$out_sg$pareto_frontier
stopifnot(nrow(ci_front) == nrow(pf), sum(pf$N == mr$n_selected & abs(pf$hr - mr$naive$est) < 1e-6) == 1)
print(plot_pareto_frontier(fs, ci_table = ci_front, show_band = TRUE, effect_neighborhood = 0.20))

The inference table, by mr_estimates_table() from the forestsearch() result alone. Two sets are bounded, both among the non-region patients: \(\hat H\) (row Qstnbl) and \(\hat H^c\), its non-region complement (row Recmnd). \(\hat H^c\) is not \(\hat G\); the region’s outcomes play no part.

Code 
mr_tab <- mr_estimates_table(fs, est.scale = "hr", digits = 3)
mv <- attr(mr_tab, "mr_values")
cc <- mr$complement; fl <- mr$field
stopifnot(near(mv$naive_est, c(mr$naive$est, cc$naive$est), 1e-12),
          near(mv$field_bound, c(fl$lower_1s, fl$complement$upper_1s), 1e-12),
          near(mv$bonferroni_bound, c(fl$joint$bonf_lower_H, fl$joint$bonf_upper_Hc), 1e-12))

3 Identified subgroup: {z_cd40 <= 236} & !{z_preanti <= 196}
Note: Med = Median survival time (months). RMSTd = Restricted mean survival time difference.

Read by location: the naive hazard ratio of \(\hat H\) is 2.661 and its de-biased value 1.629, but the field lower bound is 0.850, below 0.90: once the selection is accounted for, the data do not rule out a modest benefit in \(\hat H\). The field upper bound for \(\hat H^c\) is 0.904, below 1.0: the non-region patients outside \(\hat H\) benefit. \(\hat H\) is re-selected on a share 0.186 of the draws. With your trial: nothing changes; compute_frontier_cis() and mr_estimates_table() take your forestsearch() result.

NoteReading the bounds

mr_estimates_table() needs only the forestsearch() result run with mr_inference = TRUE. Read the field lower bound for \(\hat H\) by its location against the hazard ratios that would matter clinically in your setting: a lower bound well below 1.0 leaves benefit in \(\hat H\) open; one near or above 0.90 says that, after accounting for the selection, little benefit remains there. Read the field upper bound for \(\hat H^c\) the same way: below 1.0 says the non-region patients outside \(\hat H\) benefit. Use the Bonferroni pair when both statements are made together. The naive estimate in \(\hat H\) is selected and is not a bound. The re-selection share \(\hat p(\hat H)\) is a stability diagnostic: a small share says another rule would often have been declared from similar data.

These bounds are for sets among the non-region patients. The region’s fits on the whole region and on \(\hat G\) are ordinary Wald fits on sets defined by a fixed rule, with the region’s few events; read their intervals by location as well.

Because replicate 5 is simulated, its \(\hat H\) can also be set against \(H^*\) and its estimates against their limits; that needs the simulation design, and is in Section 4.5.

3 Setting up simulations from your own trial

This section treats rep5_trial.csv as if it were your trial, with its region observed: the column z_region is taken as recorded, and nothing about who is in the region is modelled. \(H^*\) and the effects in the cells are then your statements. Five steps, in order.

1. A data-generating mechanism that carries the observed region. inject_mrct_structure(), the function of the report’s build (Section 4.1), is given the trial and region = list(observed = "region"): with region$observed, the region is carried through the expansion with the covariates and nothing about membership is modelled. With loghr left at NULL the region’s prognostic log hazard ratio is estimated by the Weibull AFT fit, as the other covariates’ effects are; \(H^*\), \(b\) and \(h\) are set as in the report’s build (spline_spec gives \(b\) everywhere, x3 defines \(H^*\) = CD4 \(\le\) 230 and multiplies the hazard ratio in it by \(h/b\)), and the super-population is expanded by the copula. There is no scale_dgm_hazard() step here: the trial’s own data carry its hazard scale (replicate 5 was drawn with all hazards multiplied by 3), and the AFT fit to it estimates that scale.

Code 
own <- rd("rep5_trial.csv")
own <- own[, setdiff(names(own), c("id", "flag_harm"))]   # your trial has no flag_harm
names(own) <- sub("^z_", "", names(own))                   # plain names; the build adds z_
build_own <- function(h, b = 0.55, cut = 230) {
  w <- character(0)
  dgm <- withCallingHandlers(                              # warnings recorded and shown
    inject_mrct_structure(
      own,
      outcome_var = "y_sim", event_var = "event_sim", treatment_var = "treat_sim",
      continuous_vars = c("age", "wtkg", "karnof", "preanti", "cd40", "cd80"),
      factor_vars = c("hemo", "homo", "drugs", "race", "gender", "symptom"),
      x_pred = "cd40",
      spline_spec = list(knot = 300, zeta = 800, log_hrs = rep(log(b), 3)),      # b
      region = list(observed = "region"),                                        # r estimated
      x3 = list(vars = "cd40", cuts = list(cd40 = cut), loghr = log(h / b)),     # h in H*
      n_super = 20000, expand = "copula", seed = 7L,
      continuous_vars_cens = c("age", "cd40"), factor_vars_cens = "symptom"),
    warning = function(cnd) w <<- c(w, conditionMessage(cnd)))
  attr(dgm, "build_warnings") <- w
  dgm
}
t_own <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
dgm_own <- build_own(h = 2)

Every patient’s log hazard ratio is \(\log 0.55\) outside \(H^*\) and \(\log 2\) inside it. The region’s prognostic log hazard ratio, estimated from the trial, is -1.541 (\(e^{r}\) = 0.214); the mechanism that generated replicate 5 used \(r = -\log 4\) = -1.386 (Section 4.1). The region is 19.6% of the super-population and 19.4% of the trial. The build took 0.2 seconds. Its 3 warnings, shown above, come from the censoring model’s fit: every censoring time in this trial lies between 29.01 and 39.98 months, that is, all censoring is administrative, and the Weibull fit to it does not converge. Trials are drawn below with cens_adjust = 50, which pushes that model far beyond the window, so all censoring is again administrative.

2. \(H^*\) and the cells. The build above is one cell: S2’s \(h = 2\) in \(H^*\) = CD4 \(\le\) 230 and \(b = 0.55\) outside it. The other cells change only \(h\) (shown, not run):

Code 
h_cells <- c(N0 = 0.55, N1 = 0.75, S1 = 1, S2 = 2, S3 = 3, S4 = 4)   # h in H*; b = 0.55 outside
dgms_own <- lapply(h_cells, build_own)
Note4.3a — Choosing the cells

A cell is one data-generating mechanism: your trial’s build with a stated \(H^*\), a hazard ratio \(h\) inside it and \(b\) outside it, in every region. Choose \(h\) as the sizes of harm you want the strategy to be able to explain, and keep cells in which there is nothing harmful to find (\(h = b\); \(h\) between \(b\) and 1; \(h = 1\)): those are where the strategy explains a trigger that has no trial-wide explanation, and the rate at which it does so is a result to report.

3. The analytic layer on that mechanism. The four truths of the region, the non-region patients and \(G^*\), and the design probabilities at \(n = 1{,}000\), with this trial’s analysis at 40 months and entry over 11.

Code 
pop_own <- ahr_population(dgm_own, analysis_time = 40, max_entry = 11)
sets_own <- c(region = "region", nonregion = "non-region", region_Gstar = "G* (region minus H*)")
lim_own <- lapply(setNames(names(sets_own), names(sets_own)),
                  function(s) ahr_limit(pop_own, s, b = 0.55, h = 2, variance = FALSE))
p_own <- ahr_design(pop_own, b = 0.55, h = 2, n = 1000)$prob
tab_own <- rbind(
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sets_own), function(s) { e <- lim_own[[s]]
    data.frame(row = sets_own[[s]], a = f3(e$hr), b = f3(e$marghr_inf), c = f3(e$ahr), d = f3(e$cde)) })),
  data.frame(row = c("P(trigger), n = 1,000", "P(oracle joint), n = 1,000"),
             a = f3(c(p_own[["p_trigger"]], p_own[["p_trigger_and_Gstar_lt1"]])), b = "", c = "", d = ""))
knitr::kable(setNames(tab_own, c("", "margHR(40)", "margHR(∞)", "AHR", "CDE")), row.names = FALSE,

Note4.3b — The analytic layer

ahr_population() on each cell’s mechanism, with your analysis time and entry period, then ahr_limit() on the sets you care about gives each set’s four truths: read margHR at the analysis time as what the set’s Cox estimate converges to, and the AHR and CDE as the effect in the set. ahr_design() at your trial size gives P(ITT ub < 1.0), P(region ITT > 1.0), P(trigger) and the oracle joint before any simulation; if P(trigger) is very small, the campaign will have few triggered trials to summarise. ahr_solve() places one free parameter so that P(trigger) reaches a target (Section 4.3.1). These are computed by quadrature and take seconds per cell.

4. The campaign. One mrct_region_sims() call per cell, with the identifier’s arguments of Section 2 (shown, not run; no campaign is run in this section):

Code 
res_own <- mrct_region_sims(
  dgm_own, n_sims = 10000, n_sample = 1000, region_var = "z_region",
  sg_focus = "hrMaxSG", maxk = 2,
  hr.threshold = 0.90, hr.consistency = 0.80, pconsistency.threshold = 0.90,
  confounders.name = analysis_covariates(dgm_own, "observed"),   # all z_ but z_region
  conf_force = character(0),
  fs_args = list(conf.cont_jcuts = list(z_cd40 = 10, z_wtkg = 10, z_preanti = 10),
                 effect_neighborhood = 0.20, use_grf = FALSE, use_lasso = FALSE),
  sim_args = list(rand_ratio = 1, draw_treatment = TRUE, max_entry = 11, cens_adjust = 50),
  analysis_time = 40, cens_adjust = 50,
  parallel_args = list(plan = "multisession", workers = 64, show_message = FALSE),
  details = FALSE, seed = 20261102, record = "full")
Note4.3c — The campaign

Give mrct_region_sims() your cell’s mechanism, your trial size, your region variable and the identifier’s arguments you used in Section 2; sim_args and analysis_time carry the entry, window and dropout of the design. Keep record = "full": case selection reads the per-trial Cox fits it stores. Give each cell its own seed and record it: a replicate is redrawn from the mechanism, the call seed and its index. Before a full campaign, time a short run at the worker count you will use; the time per trial on a lightly loaded machine does not carry over to all workers busy.

5. Case selection and the summaries conditional on the trigger (shown, not run): the shares of the triggered trials, from the per-trial Cox fits of the full record, and a case chosen by the rule of Section 4.4.

Code 
e <- as.data.frame(attr(res_own, "estimators")); r <- as.data.frame(res_own)
fit_of <- function(k) e[e$estimator == k, ][match(r$sim, e$sim[e$estimator == k]), ]
itt <- fit_of("itt_all"); rgn <- fit_of("itt_region"); gh <- fit_of("region_Ghat"); gs <- fit_of("region_Gstar")
lt1 <- function(v) !is.na(v) & v < 1
K <- lt1(itt$hi) & !is.na(rgn$hr) & rgn$hr > 1               # the trigger
dec <- r$any_found == 1
c(triggered = sum(K), declared = mean(dec[K]), joint = mean(dec[K] & lt1(gh$hr[K])),
  oracle_joint = mean(lt1(gs$hr[K])))
case_own <- mrct_select_case(res_own)                         # the first trial meeting the rule
Note4.3d — Reading the results

Summarise the campaign conditional on the trigger: a team runs the joint analysis only when the trial is positive and the region’s estimate is above 1.0, so the triggered trials are the denominator that matters. Report for each cell the share of triggered trials with a declaration, the joint and, beside it, the oracle joint as the benchmark that removing \(H^*\) exactly would give under the stated mechanism (a benchmark, not a bound: in a given trial \(\hat G\) can do better); then the same rows in the null cells. mrct_select_case() picks a case by a stated rule before it is looked at, and mrct_case_study() redraws and examines it (Section 4.4).

4 How replicate 5 was generated: the report’s simulation design

Replicate 5 is one trial drawn from the report’s S2 cell. This section is that design: the data-generating mechanism built from ACTG 175 (Section 4.1), the eight cells, the analytic layer (Section 4.3), and the rule and the calls by which replicate 5 was found and redrawn (Section 4.4); it closes with what can be said about replicate 5 only because it is simulated (Section 4.5).

4.1 The data-generating mechanism, built from ACTG 175

A Weibull accelerated-failure-time model is fitted to a published trial and expanded to a super-population of 20,000 rows by a Gaussian copula. A region of about 20% of patients is planted by a logistic model with odds ratio 3 on symptomatic status and no CD4 term, and its baseline hazard is shifted by \(r\); every patient’s hazard ratio is \(b = 0.55\) outside \(H^*\) = {CD4 \(\le\) 230} and \(h\) inside it, in every region; all hazards are then multiplied by \(m = 3\). Three calls build it, shown here as a reader would make them with their own trial.

1. The trial data. ACTG 175 (speff2trial), arms ZDV + ddI (arms == 1, experimental) and ddI alone (arms == 3, control). The outcome is days to the composite endpoint, in months, with event indicator cens; the prognostic covariates are age, weight (wtkg), Karnofsky score (karnof), days of prior antiretroviral therapy (preanti), baseline CD4 (cd40) and CD8 (cd80) counts, and the binary haemophilia (hemo), homosexual activity (homo), drug use (drugs), race, gender and symptomatic status (symptom).

Code 
actg <- subset(speff2trial::ACTG175, arms %in% c(1L, 3L))
actg$treat_mrct <- as.integer(actg$arms == 1L)   # ZDV + ddI = 1, ddI = 0
actg$time_months <- actg$days / 30.4375
rownames(actg) <- NULL
c(patients = nrow(actg), events = sum(actg$cens), experimental = sum(actg$treat_mrct))
    patients       events experimental 
        1083          231          522

2. The region and the harmed subgroup. inject_mrct_structure() fits the Weibull model on the twelve covariates, expands it by the copula, plants the region (region: prevalence, the logistic model’s odds ratios, the prognostic log hazard ratio \(r\)) and the harmed subgroup (spline_spec sets \(b\) everywhere; x3 multiplies it by \(h/b\) in CD4 \(\le\) 230), here for cell S2 (\(h = 2\)). The copula’s latent correlation is fitted live by latentcor (Suggests); without latentcor the call warns and uses the normal-score correlation instead, which gives a valid but different super-population.

Code 
dgm_live <- inject_mrct_structure(
  actg,
  outcome_var = "time_months", event_var = "cens", treatment_var = "treat_mrct",
  continuous_vars = c("age", "wtkg", "karnof", "preanti", "cd40", "cd80"),
  factor_vars = c("hemo", "homo", "drugs", "race", "gender", "symptom"),
  x_pred = "cd40",
  spline_spec = list(knot = 300, zeta = 800, log_hrs = rep(log(0.55), 3)),  # b = 0.55
  region = list(prevalence = 0.20, or_pred = 1, x1_vars = "symptom", or_x1 = 3,
                loghr = -log(4),                                          # r
                band = list(cut = 230, or = 1)),
  x3 = list(vars = "cd40", cuts = list(cd40 = 230), loghr = log(2 / 0.55)),  # h = 2 in H*
  region_treat_loghr = NULL,
  n_super = 20000, expand = "copula", seed = 7L,
  continuous_vars_cens = c("age", "cd40"), factor_vars_cens = "symptom")

3. The hazard scale. scale_dgm_hazard() multiplies every hazard by \(m\) and leaves every hazard ratio unchanged.

Code 
dgm_live <- scale_dgm_hazard(dgm_live, m = 3)
c(rows = nrow(dgm_live$df_super), region = mean(dgm_live$df_super$z_region),
  Hstar = mean(dgm_live$df_super$flag_harm))
     rows    region     Hstar 
2.000e+04 2.006e-01 1.569e-01

To use your own trial, change these and nothing else:

  • the data frame and its outcome, event and treatment names (outcome_var, event_var, treatment_var; treatment coded 1 = experimental);
  • the covariates (continuous_vars, factor_vars, binary factors coded 0/1, and the censoring model’s continuous_vars_cens, factor_vars_cens);
  • the region model (region: its prevalence, the covariates that predict membership and their odds ratios, its prognostic log hazard ratio \(r\));
  • \(H^*\) and its effects: the covariate and cut that define it (x3, region$band), \(b\) outside it (spline_spec$log_hrs) and \(h\) inside it (x3$loghr \(= \log(h/b)\));
  • the analysis window and entry: the analysis time and the uniform entry period used below (analysis_time = 40, max_entry = 11), and cens_adjust for the dropout model.
NoteReproducing this report’s build exactly

This chunk exists only so that the committed record is reproduced to the last digit on any platform: it builds the cells with the latent correlation stored with the campaign’s build (latent_R.csv, passed as latent_R), so no latentcor fit is made. A reader never needs it. Everything from the build check onward uses the cells built here (build_cell()).

Code 
latent_R <- as.matrix(rd("latent_R.csv", row.names = 1))

# One cell: hazard ratio h in H* = {CD4 <= 230}, b = 0.55 elsewhere, region
# prognostic log-HR r, all hazards x m; the calls of steps 2 and 3 above.
build_cell <- function(h, r = -log(4), b = 0.55, cut = 230, m = 3) {
  w <- character(0)
  dgm <- withCallingHandlers(
    inject_mrct_structure(
      actg,
      outcome_var = "time_months", event_var = "cens", treatment_var = "treat_mrct",
      continuous_vars = c("age", "wtkg", "karnof", "preanti", "cd40", "cd80"),
      factor_vars = c("hemo", "homo", "drugs", "race", "gender", "symptom"),
      x_pred = "cd40",
      spline_spec = list(knot = 300, zeta = 800, log_hrs = rep(log(b), 3)),
      region = list(prevalence = 0.20, or_pred = 1, x1_vars = "symptom", or_x1 = 3,
                    loghr = r, band = list(cut = cut, or = 1)),
      x3 = list(vars = "cd40", cuts = list(cd40 = cut), loghr = log(h / b)),
      region_treat_loghr = NULL,
      n_super = 20000, expand = "copula", seed = 7L,
      continuous_vars_cens = c("age", "cd40"), factor_vars_cens = "symptom",
      latent_R = latent_R),
    warning = function(cnd) { w <<- c(w, conditionMessage(cnd)); invokeRestart("muffleWarning") })
  dgm <- scale_dgm_hazard(dgm, m = m)
  attr(dgm, "build_warnings") <- w
  dgm
}
t_build <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
dgm_S2 <- build_cell(h = 2)
t_build <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t_build
# the live fit of step 2 against the shipped matrix
R_live <- dgm_live$mrct$latent_R
R_diff <- if (is.null(R_live)) NA_real_ else max(abs(R_live[rownames(latent_R), colnames(latent_R)] - latent_R))
live_same <- isTRUE(R_diff == 0) && identical(dgm_live$df_super, dgm_S2$df_super)
c(seconds = round(t_build, 1), rows = nrow(dgm_S2$df_super), latent_R_max_abs_diff = R_diff,
  super_population_identical = live_same)

Code

Passed: the build equals the record (largest relative difference 6.7e-15). In this build the region holds 20.1% of the super-population, \(H^*\) holds 15.7% of all patients (16.5% of the region and 15.5% outside it), and at equal covariates a region patient has \(e^{r}\) = 0.25 times the hazard of a non-region patient. The trial: \(n = 1{,}000\), 1:1, entry uniform over 11 months, analysis at 40 months; the Weibull dropout is pushed far beyond the window (cens_adjust = 50), so all censoring is administrative.

4.2 The cells

Six cells at \(r = -\log 4\) differ only in the hazard ratio \(h\) inside \(H^*\); two later-enrolling cells keep S2’s effects and let the region enter later, with \(r\) or the delay solved so that P(trigger) = 0.25 (Section 4.3.1). The specifications as the committed runs’ timing records state them:

Code 
tf <- rd("timing_full.csv"); ts1 <- rd("timing_S1.csv"); te <- rd("timing_entry_cells.csv")
cells <- rbind(
  data.frame(cell = sub("_rmlog4$", "", tf$setting), h = tf$h, r = -log(4), delay = 0, n = 1000,
             replicates = tf$replicates, seed = tf$seed),
  data.frame(cell = "S1", h = ts1$h[ts1$setting == "S1_rmlog4"], r = -log(4), delay = 0, n = 1000,
             replicates = ts1$replicates[ts1$setting == "S1_rmlog4"], seed = ts1$seed[ts1$setting == "S1_rmlog4"]),
  data.frame(cell = te$setting, h = te$h, r = te$r, delay = te$a, n = te$n, replicates = te$replicates,
             seed = te$seed))
cells <- cells[match(c("N0", "N1", "S1", "S2", "S3", "S4", "S2_D1", "S2_D2"), cells$cell), ]
rownames(cells) <- NULL
# the shipped build record's h and r for the five full cells

4.3 The analytic layer in brief

For any patient set of such a DGM, analysed at a calendar time with uniform staggered entry and administrative censoring only, the analytic layer computes by quadrature (nothing is drawn) the exact limit of the two-sample Cox estimate on the set (the Struthers–Kalbfleisch root, margHR(40)), its information and robust variance, the expected events, the correlation between nested sets’ estimates, the set’s AHR and CDE, and the normal-approximation probability of the trigger at a trial size. ahr_population() reads the DGM; ahr_limit() gives a set’s four truths; ahr_design() gives the trial-level probabilities; ahr_solve() solves P(trigger) = target in one free parameter. Section 6 states the formulas.

Code 
t_an <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
cells6 <- cells[cells$delay == 0, ]
dgms <- lapply(setNames(cells6$h, cells6$cell), function(h) if (h == 2) dgm_S2 else build_cell(h = h))
pops <- lapply(dgms, ahr_population, analysis_time = 40, max_entry = 11)
sets4 <- c(all = "all patients", nonregion = "non-region", region = "region", region_Gstar = "G* (region minus H*)")
truths <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pops), function(k) {
  h <- cells6$h[cells6$cell == k]
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sets4), function(s) {
    e <- ahr_limit(pops[[k]], s, b = 0.55, h = h, variance = FALSE)
    data.frame(cell = k, set = s, marghr_40 = e$hr, marghr_inf = e$marghr_inf, ahr = e$ahr, cde = e$cde)
  }))
}))
# against the committed predictions (the analytic records of the campaign)
pred <- rbind(rd("predictions_full.csv"), rd("predictions_S1.csv"))
pv <- function(cell, q, set) { v <- pred$value[pred$cell == cell & pred$quantity == q & pred$set == set]; stopifnot(length(v) == 1); v }
tr_ref <- mapply(function(c, s, q) pv(paste0(c, "_rmlog4"), q, s),
                 rep(truths$cell, 4), rep(truths$set, 4),
                 rep(c("marghr_40", "marghr_inf", "ahr", "cde"), each = nrow(truths)))
stopifnot(near(unlist(truths[c("marghr_40", "marghr_inf", "ahr", "cde")]), tr_ref))
tt <- truths
tt$set <- sets4[tt$set]; tt[3:6] <- lapply(tt[3:6], f3)
reg_S2 <- truths[truths$cell == "S2" & truths$set == "region", ]
stopifnot(reg_S2$marghr_40 < 1, reg_S2$cde > 1)
knitr::kable(setNames(tt, c("cell", "set", "margHR(40)", "margHR(∞)", "AHR", "CDE")), row.names = FALSE,
             align = "llrrrr", caption = "The four truths of four sets in the six cells at r = −log 4 (ahr_limit()); equal to the committed predictions to 1e-9.")

The four truths differ, and the difference is the point. The AHR and the CDE depend on a set only through its \(H^*\) shares; the two marginal ratios are bounded in \(h\) and depend on the window and the prognostic structure. In S2 the region’s margHR(40) is 0.868, below 1, although its CDE is 1.097: the trigger in S2 is a sampling event around a regional limit below 1.

The trigger predictions at \(n = 1{,}000\), and the oracle joint, P(trigger and region(\(G^*\)) < 1.0):

Code 
design_tab <- function(n, cells_k, pops_k, ref_cell) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(names(pops_k), function(k) {
    h <- cells_k$h[cells_k$cell == k]
    p <- ahr_design(pops_k[[k]], b = 0.55, h = h, n = n)$prob
    data.frame(cell = k, n = n, p_A = p[["p_itt_ub_lt1"]], p_B = p[["p_region_itt_gt1"]],
               p_A_B = p[["p_trigger"]], p_Cstar = p[["p_region_Gstar_lt1"]],
               p_A_B_Cstar = p[["p_trigger_and_Gstar_lt1"]], ref = ref_cell(k))
  }))
}
d1000 <- design_tab(1000, cells6, pops, function(k) paste0(k, "_rmlog4"))

  stopifnot(all(abs(d1000[[q]] - vapply(d1000$ref, function(cc) pv(cc, q, ""), 0)) < 1e-9))

  `P(region(G*) < 1.0)` = f3(d$p_Cstar), `P(oracle joint)` = f3(d$p_A_B_Cstar),
  `P(G* < 1.0 | trigger)` = f3(d$p_A_B_Cstar / d$p_A_B), check.names = FALSE),
  row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrr")

4.3.1 How \(r = -\log 4\) was chosen, and the later-enrolling regions

The campaign’s regional shift was chosen to make the trigger frequent at the design: with S2’s effects (\(h = 2\)), \(r\) solving P(trigger) = 0.25 at \(n = 1{,}000\) is found by ahr_solve(), and the campaign rounded it to \(-\log 4\). Each evaluation rebuilds the DGM at that \(r\).

Code 
p_trig_r <- function(r, delay = NULL) {
  d <- build_cell(h = 2, r = r)
  ahr_design(ahr_population(d, 40, 11, entry_delay = delay), b = 0.55, h = 2, n = 1000)$prob[["p_trigger"]]
}
roots <- rd("entry_roots.csv")
rref <- function(tag) { x <- roots[startsWith(roots$row, tag), ]; stopifnot(nrow(x) == 1); x }
sol_r <- ahr_solve(p_trig_r, 0.25, c(-log(5), -log(3.5)), n_scan = 5L, tol = 1e-10)
ref0 <- rref("Reference: a = 0, r solving")
stopifnot(sol_r$n_roots == 1, abs(sol_r$roots - ref0$r) < 1e-6)
c(root_r = sol_r$roots, k_in_minus_log_k = exp(-sol_r$roots), committed_root = ref0$r,
  P_trigger_at_root = sol_r$values)
           root_r  k_in_minus_log_k    committed_root P_trigger_at_root 
        -1.441190          4.225721         -1.441190          0.250000

The root is \(r = -\log 4.226\), the committed -1.4412; the campaign used \(r = -\log 4\), where P(trigger) is 0.241. The same target defines the two later-enrolling cells, in which the region’s patients enter \(a\) months after the others (entry_delay): D1 keeps \(r = -\log 2\) and solves the delay \(a\); D2 fixes \(a = 6\) months and solves \(r\).

Code 
dgm_r2 <- build_cell(h = 2, r = -log(2))
p_trig_a <- function(a) ahr_design(ahr_population(dgm_r2, 40, 11, entry_delay = list(var = "z_region", delay = a)),
                                   b = 0.55, h = 2, n = 1000)$prob[["p_trigger"]]
sol_a <- ahr_solve(p_trig_a, 0.25, c(11, 12), scan = c(11, 12), tol = 1e-8)
sol_r6 <- ahr_solve(p_trig_r, 0.25, c(-log(3.5), -log(2.5)), n_scan = 5L, tol = 1e-10,
                    delay = list(var = "z_region", delay = 6))
d1r <- rref("D1:"); d2r <- rref("D2:")
stopifnot(sol_a$n_roots == 1, abs(sol_a$roots - d1r$a) < 1e-6,
          sol_r6$n_roots == 1, abs(sol_r6$roots - d2r$r) < 1e-6)
# the design layer at the two roots, against the committed root records
dD <- lapply(list(S2_D1 = list(r = -log(2), a = sol_a$roots), S2_D2 = list(r = sol_r6$roots, a = 6)), function(x) {
  d <- if (abs(x$r + log(2)) < 1e-12) dgm_r2 else build_cell(h = 2, r = x$r)
  ahr_design(ahr_population(d, 40, 11, entry_delay = list(var = "z_region", delay = x$a)), 0.55, 2, 1000)
})
for (k in names(dD)) {
  x <- if (k == "S2_D1") d1r else d2r; p <- dD[[k]]$prob
  stopifnot(abs(p[["p_itt_ub_lt1"]] - x$p_itt_ub_lt1) < 1e-6, abs(p[["p_region_itt_gt1"]] - x$p_region_itt_gt1) < 1e-6,
            abs(p[["p_trigger_and_Gstar_lt1"]] - x$p_trigger_Gstar_lt1) < 1e-6)
}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  cell = c("S2_D1", "S2_D2"), `r` = sprintf("−log %s", f3(exp(-c(-log(2), sol_r6$roots)))),
  `region delay a (months)` = f3(c(sol_a$roots, 6)),
  `P(ITT ub < 1.0)` = f3(vapply(dD, function(d) d$prob[["p_itt_ub_lt1"]], 0)),
  `P(region ITT > 1.0)` = f3(vapply(dD, function(d) d$prob[["p_region_itt_gt1"]], 0)),
  `P(trigger)` = f3(vapply(dD, function(d) d$prob[["p_trigger"]], 0)),
  `P(oracle joint)` = f3(vapply(dD, function(d) d$prob[["p_trigger_and_Gstar_lt1"]], 0)),
  `region margHR(40)` = f3(vapply(dD, function(d) d$sets$marghr[d$sets$set == "region"], 0)),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrrr",
  caption = "The later-enrolling cells: roots reproduced with entry_delay (committed roots to 1e-6).")
The later-enrolling cells: roots reproduced with entry_delay (committed roots to 1e-6).
cell r region delay a (months) P(ITT ub < 1.0) P(region ITT > 1.0) P(trigger) P(oracle joint) region margHR(40)

Code 
t_an <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t_an

A later-enrolling region is followed for less time, which keeps its 40-month window in the phase where the treated \(H^*\) patients are failing: a delay of 11.62 months at \(r = -\log 2\), or of 6 months at \(r = -\log 2.946\), does what the shift to \(-\log 4\) does at no delay. The analytic computations of this section took 10 seconds.

4.4 Finding a case study

The report’s case example is one trial of the S2 cell, chosen by a stated rule: the first replicate, by index, that reaches the trigger, declares \(\hat H\) and has region(\(\hat G\)) < 1.0. Four calls find and examine such a trial in any simulation. They are shown on S2 with the campaign’s arguments and call seed at 100 replicates (nsims_demo, set at the top of the file), on workers from parallel::detectCores(); with the campaign’s seed these replicates are the campaign’s first 100. The same run is summarised beside the campaign in Section 5.6.

1. Simulate with the full record. mrct_region_sims(record = "full") keeps, for every trial, the Cox fits of the patient sets (the "estimators" attribute) that the selection reads.

Code 
seed_S2 <- cells$seed[cells$cell == "S2"]
confounders <- analysis_covariates(dgm_S2, "observed")
workers_demo <- max(1L, min(parallel::detectCores(), nsims_demo))
t_demo <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
demo <- mrct_region_sims(
  dgm_S2, n_sims = nsims_demo, n_sample = 1000, region_var = "z_region",
  sg_focus = "hrMaxSG", maxk = 2,
  hr.threshold = 0.90, hr.consistency = 0.80, pconsistency.threshold = 0.90,
  confounders.name = confounders, conf_force = character(0),
  fs_args = list(conf.cont_jcuts = list(z_cd40 = 10, z_wtkg = 10, z_preanti = 10),
                 effect_neighborhood = 0.20, use_grf = FALSE, use_lasso = FALSE),
  sim_args = list(rand_ratio = 1, draw_treatment = TRUE, max_entry = 11, cens_adjust = 50),
  analysis_time = 40, cens_adjust = 50,
  parallel_args = list(plan = "multisession", workers = workers_demo, show_message = FALSE),
  details = FALSE, verbose_n_sims = 0, seed = seed_S2, record = "full")
t_demo <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t_demo
future::plan(future::sequential)

3. Redraw it, and check it against Section 2. mrct_case_study() redraws trial k exactly as the simulation drew it (under L’Ecuyer-CMRG, by simulate_from_dgm() with seed equal to the call seed plus \(k\), restoring R’s default generator after), runs the identifier on its non-region patients with the simulation’s arguments (the arguments mrct_region_sims() takes directly go into fs_args here) and analyses the four sets. It runs here with mr_inference = FALSE: the MR draws are made once, in Section 2.3. The redrawn trial must equal the shipped rep5_trial.csv in every shipped column, to floating-point precision (see the note below the check), and its \(\hat H\) and four sets those of Section 2; the article stops otherwise.

Code 
t_cs <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]

  dgm_S2, seed = seed_S2, k = case$sim, n = 1000, region_var = "z_region",

                 hr.threshold = 0.90, hr.consistency = 0.80, pconsistency.threshold = 0.90,

                 conf.cont_jcuts = list(z_cd40 = 10, z_wtkg = 10, z_preanti = 10),

  sim_args = list(rand_ratio = 1, draw_treatment = TRUE, max_entry = 11, cens_adjust = 50),
  analysis_time = 40, cens_adjust = 50,
  mr_inference = FALSE)

NotePlatform precision

rep5_trial.csv was written on the Linux machine that ran the campaign. On another platform the redraw is the same trial, but continuous columns can differ in their last digits, because the linear-algebra library and floating-point arithmetic differ. On macOS (arm64, R 4.5.2, Apple’s Accelerate library), two columns differ, y_sim and z_wtkg, by at most 5e-15 relative, and every integer and 0/1 column is identical. The check therefore compares with a relative tolerance of 1e-12, not exactly.

plot(cs, which = "forest")

The selection returns replicate 5, the report’s case example and the trial of Section 2.

4.5 Because this trial is simulated

With a real trial none of this is available: \(H^*\) is unknown, so there is no \(G^*\), no oracle and no sensitivity or specificity. This subsection uses the S2 build and the analytic layer, so it is placed here, after them, rather than in Section 2.

4.5.1 \(\hat H\) against \(H^*\), in the region and outside

Code 
cc2 <- function(w) c(TP = sum(in_Hhat[w] & Hstar[w]), FP = sum(in_Hhat[w] & !Hstar[w]),
                     FN = sum(!in_Hhat[w] & Hstar[w]), TN = sum(!in_Hhat[w] & !Hstar[w]))
cf_non <- cc2(!reg); cf_reg <- cc2(reg)
stopifnot(identical(cf_non, cs$confusion$nonregion), identical(cf_reg, cs$confusion$region))
sens <- function(x) x[["TP"]] / (x[["TP"]] + x[["FN"]]); spec <- function(x) x[["TN"]] / (x[["TN"]] + x[["FP"]])
knitr::kable(data.frame(population = c("non-region (where the identifier ran)", "region (where Ĥ is applied)"),
                        n = c(sum(!reg), sum(reg)),

Code 
hr4 <- setNames(four$hr, four$set)
stopifnot(hr4[["region_Gstar"]] < hr4[["region_Ghat"]], hr4[["region_Ghat"]] < 1, hr4[["itt_region"]] > 1)

\(\hat H\) has the right variable and nearly the right cut, narrowed by prior therapy: it finds about half of the harmed patients (Sens 0.500 outside the region) and almost no one else (Spec 0.988). Applied in the region it removes 20 patients, 18 of them in \(H^*\), and region(\(\hat G\)) is 0.844, between the whole region and the oracle region(\(G^*\)) = 0.736, as a partial removal of \(H^*\) should.

4.5.3 The four sets beside their limits

The analytic layer’s limit of each set’s Cox estimate, with the set’s AHR and CDE; \(\hat G\) is replicate 5’s rule applied to every super-population row of the region. \(z\) is the estimate’s distance from its limit in units of the robust SE that the limit implies at the set’s size.

Code

                 region_Ghat = pop_S2$region & !Hhat_super)

The region’s limit, margHR(40) = 0.868, is below 1; replicate 5’s regional estimate sits 0.56 robust SDs above it. A regional prognostic effect, a harmed subgroup and a finite window move the region’s limit toward 1, and sampling did the rest.

5 Simulation results

The campaign ran 10,000 replicates per cell at \(n = 1{,}000\) with mrct_region_sims(). Its records are summarised here from the shipped core tables; Section 5.6 summarises the small run of Section 4.4 beside them.

Every count-derived entry equals its recount from the numeric records. Reading: the trigger becomes more frequent as the harm in \(H^*\) grows (from 540 triggered trials in N0 to 3,048 in S4). Where there is something to find (S2–S4) a subgroup is declared in essentially every triggered trial, it overlaps \(H^*\) with sensitivity about 0.6 and specificity above 0.95, and the joint holds in 51.2% to 61.6% of triggered trials, against an oracle benchmark of 77.7% to 89.2%. Where there is nothing harmful to find (N0) a subgroup is still declared in 52.2% of triggered trials and the joint holds in 10.6%: the strategy “explains” some triggers when there is nothing to explain, which is why it is signal generation.

mv_ <- function(row, k) mfc[[k]][mfc$row == row]
stopifnot(max(vapply(c("N0", "N1", "S1"), mv_, 0, row = "lb_090")) < 1)

Reading: where there is nothing harmful to find (N0, N1, S1) the lower bound for \(\hat H\) almost never excludes a hazard ratio of 0.90 (0.30% at most): the bound does not mistake a selected subgroup for a harmed one. With harm \(h = 2\) (S2) it excludes 0.90 in 18.70% of declared triggered trials and 1.0 in 13.60%; with \(h = 4\) in 88.90% and 83.90%. The upper bound for \(\hat H^c\) is below 1.0 in every cell’s declared triggered trials (100.00% at least): the patients outside \(\hat H\) benefit. The spread between the de-biased estimate and the bound is the price of the selection.

5.5 The campaign code and its wall-clock

The committed campaign, one mrct_region_sims() call per cell, with every argument (shown, not run):

Code 
campaign_cell <- function(dgm, seed, n_sims = 10000L, workers = 64L, entry_delay = NULL) {
  mrct_region_sims(
    dgm, n_sims = n_sims, n_sample = 1000, region_var = "z_region",
    sg_focus = "hrMaxSG", maxk = 2,
    hr.threshold = 0.90, hr.consistency = 0.80, pconsistency.threshold = 0.90,
    confounders.name = analysis_covariates(dgm, "observed"), conf_force = character(0),
    fs_args = list(conf.cont_jcuts = list(z_cd40 = 10, z_wtkg = 10, z_preanti = 10),
                   effect_neighborhood = 0.20, use_grf = FALSE, use_lasso = FALSE),
    sim_args = list(rand_ratio = 1, draw_treatment = TRUE, max_entry = 11, cens_adjust = 50,
                    entry_delay = entry_delay),
    analysis_time = 40, cens_adjust = 50,
    parallel_args = list(plan = "multisession", workers = workers, show_message = FALSE),
    details = FALSE, seed = seed, record = "full")
}
# the six cells at r = -log 4
for (k in c("N0", "N1", "S1", "S2", "S3", "S4"))
  res[[k]] <- campaign_cell(build_cell(h = cells$h[cells$cell == k]), seed = cells$seed[cells$cell == k])
# the later-enrolling cells: the region enters a months later
res$S2_D1 <- campaign_cell(build_cell(h = 2, r = -log(2)), seed = cells$seed[cells$cell == "S2_D1"],
                           entry_delay = list(var = "z_region", delay = sol_a$roots))
res$S2_D2 <- campaign_cell(build_cell(h = 2, r = sol_r6$roots), seed = cells$seed[cells$cell == "S2_D2"],
                           entry_delay = list(var = "z_region", delay = 6))

The committed runs predate record = "full" and entry_delay: their per-replicate records were rebuilt by redrawing each trial from its seed, which record = "full" now returns directly from the same trials, and the later-enrolling cells stored a fixed entry time per super-population row (entry_var), where entry_delay redraws the entry each trial with the same law. The timing records:

            data.frame(cell = te$setting, workers = te$workers, wall_sec = te$wall_sec))

}))

5.6 The demonstration run

The run of Section 4.4 (100 replicates of S2 with the campaign’s arguments and call seed, on 14 workers, 42 seconds), summarised into the core rows by the definitions of the core table. With the campaign’s seed, its replicates are the campaign’s first 100; Section 4.4 checks its first replicates against the shipped record.

Code 
g_est <- function(k) { y <- est[est$estimator == k, ]; y[match(demo$sim, y$sim), ] }
itt <- g_est("itt_all"); rgn <- g_est("itt_region"); gh <- g_est("region_Ghat"); gs <- g_est("region_Gstar")
lt1 <- function(v) !is.na(v) & v < 1; gt1 <- function(v) !is.na(v) & v > 1
A <- lt1(itt$hi); K <- A & gt1(rgn$hr); dec <- demo$any_found == 1; DK <- dec & K
ss <- function(tp, fn) tp / (tp + fn)
sens_non <- with(demo, ss(TP_nonregion, FN_nonregion)); spec_non <- with(demo, ss(TN_nonregion, FP_nonregion))
sens_reg <- with(demo, ss(TP_region, FN_region)); spec_reg <- with(demo, ss(TN_region, FP_region))
pk <- function(w, d = K) if (sum(d)) pc(sum(w & d) / sum(d)) else "–"
av <- function(v) if (sum(DK)) pc(mean(v[DK], na.rm = TRUE)) else "–"
demo_rows <- data.frame(
  row = c("trial power (ITT ub < 1.0)", "trials reaching the trigger (count)", "subgroup declared",
          "Sens / Spec of Ĥ vs H*, non-region", "Sens / Spec of Ĥ vs H*, region",
          "declared, region(Ĝ) < 1.0", "region(G*) < 1.0", "declared, region(Ĝ) ≥ 1.0"),
  demonstration = c(pc(mean(A)), sprintf("%d of %d", sum(K), nsims_demo), pk(dec),
                    paste(av(sens_non), "/", av(spec_non)), paste(av(sens_reg), "/", av(spec_reg)),
                    pk(dec & lt1(gh$hr)), pk(lt1(gs$hr)), pk(dec & !lt1(gh$hr))),
  campaign = wide$S2)

At 100 replicates the demonstration has 20 triggered trials, so its rows carry large Monte Carlo error; they are a check of the pipeline, not an estimate of its operating characteristics. The whole article took 1.8 minutes to run.

6 Appendix: the analytic tools

This appendix condenses the analytic chapter of the technical report (Chapter 6, “The analytic layer”; theory notes AHR_mrct_dgm.qmd and AHR_complete.qmd of the mrct-consistency repository), where the derivations are.

The DGM in closed form. The Weibull AFT draws \(\log T = \mu + \ell_z(x) + \tau\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon = \log \mathrm{Exp}(1)\), so \[ \bar F(s \mid x, z) = \exp\{-\Lambda_0(s)\, e^{\theta_z(x)}\}, \qquad \Lambda_0(s) = (s e^{-\mu})^{1/\tau}, \qquad \theta_z(x) = -\ell_z(x)/\tau , \] a proportional-hazards model in \((x, z)\) with Weibull baseline. The prognostic part is \(\theta_0(x) = x^\top\beta + r\,\mathbf 1\{x \in R\}\), the treatment effect \(\psi(x) = \theta_1(x) - \theta_0(x) = \log b + \log(h/b)\,\mathbf 1\{\mathrm{CD4} \le 230\}\), and scale_dgm_hazard() sets \(\mu \leftarrow \mu_{\text{fit}} - \tau \log m\), multiplying every hazard by \(m\) and leaving every \(\theta\) unchanged.

The counting-process setting and the least-false limit. On a patient set \(\mathcal S\) with entry \(E \sim U(0, t_e)\) and analysis at calendar time \(t_a\) (here 11 and 40 months), patient \(i\) has window \(t_a - E_i\), at-risk process \(Y_i(s)\) and counting process \(N_i(s)\). The two-sample Cox estimate \(\hat\beta_{\mathcal S}\) is the root of the partial-likelihood score \(U_{n,\mathcal S}(\beta) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal S}\int_0^{t_a}\{Z_i - \bar Z_{\mathcal S}(s, \beta)\}\,dN_i(s)\), \(\bar Z_{\mathcal S} = S^{(1)}_{\mathcal S}/S^{(0)}_{\mathcal S}\). The model is misspecified (the set mixes patients with different hazard ratios), and \(\hat\beta_{\mathcal S}\) converges to the least-false parameter \(\beta^*_{\mathcal S}\), the root of the population score (Struthers and Kalbfleisch 1986; Gerds and Schumacher 2001); margHR(40) \(= e^{\beta^*_{\mathcal S}}\). Breslow’s estimator converges to \(\Lambda_0^*\), with \(\lambda_0^*/\lambda_0 = (f_1 + f_0)/(e^{\beta^*}A_1 + A_0)\) in operational time.

The Struthers–Kalbfleisch root for a patient set. In operational time \(u = \Lambda_0(s)\) patient \(i\) on arm \(z\) is exponential with rate \(e^{\theta_{z,i}}\); with \(A_z(u) = |\mathcal S|^{-1}\sum_{\mathcal S} e^{-u e^{\theta_{z,i}}}\), \(f_z = -A_z'\) and the entry factor \(H_w(u) = H(t_a - \Lambda_0^{-1}(u))\), \(H\) the entry distribution function, the limit is the unique root of \[ \begin{aligned} U_{\mathcal S}(\beta) &= \tfrac12 \int_0^{\Lambda_0(t_a)} H_w(u)\Bigl\{f_1(u) - r(u, \beta)\,[f_1(u) + f_0(u)]\Bigr\}\,du,\\ r(u, \beta) &= \frac{e^\beta A_1(u)}{e^\beta A_1(u) + A_0(u)} , \end{aligned} \] and margHR(\(\infty\)) is the root with \(H_w \equiv 1\) to \(u = \infty\). \(\partial U/\partial\beta < 0\), so the root is unique. With \(\delta(u) = \log\{A_1/A_0\}\) and the set’s instantaneous hazard ratio \(\vartheta_{\mathcal S}(u) = (f_1/A_1)/(f_0/A_0)\) the score is \(\int\{\operatorname{expit}(\log\vartheta_{\mathcal S} + \delta) - \operatorname{expit}(\beta + \delta)\}\,dN\), \(dN = \tfrac12 H_w (f_1 + f_0)\,du\): the score of a time-varying-effect model whose profile is induced by composition. ahr_limit() evaluates the arm functions as finite sums over the super-population rows of the set, integrates by composite Gauss–Legendre quadrature on geometric panels in \(u\) with breaks at the entry kinks, and finds the root by uniroot(). The set’s other truths are \[ \mathrm{AHR}(\mathcal S) = \exp\Bigl\{\tfrac1{|\mathcal S|}\textstyle\sum_{\mathcal S}\psi\Bigr\} = b^{1 - p_{\mathcal S}} h^{p_{\mathcal S}}, \qquad \mathrm{CDE}(\mathcal S) = \frac{\sum_{\mathcal S} e^{\theta_1}}{\sum_{\mathcal S} e^{\theta_0}} = (1 - \omega^0_{\mathcal S})\,b + \omega^0_{\mathcal S}\,h , \] \(p_{\mathcal S}\) the set’s \(H^*\) share and \(\omega^0_{\mathcal S}\) the share of its baseline hazard carried by \(H^*\).

The clock identity and the frailty reading. Under a uniform effect (\(h = b\)), \(A_1(u) = L_{\mathcal S}(bu)\) and \(A_0(u) = L_{\mathcal S}(u)\) with \(L_{\mathcal S}\) the Laplace transform of \(e^{\theta_0}\) over the set: the covariate-driven baseline acts as a frailty, and \(\vartheta_{\mathcal S}(s) = b\,\ell_{\mathcal S}(b\Lambda_0(s))/\ell_{\mathcal S}(\Lambda_0(s))\), with \(\ell_{\mathcal S}\) the survival-weighted mean of \(e^{\theta_0}\) among the set’s survivors, drifts from \(b\) toward 1 as high-hazard patients leave. The regional shift adds \(r\) to \(\theta_0\) on every region row, so for a set inside the region every arm function at \(r\) is the function at \(r = 0\) evaluated at \(e^r u\): \(r\) is a clock on the region. margHR(\(\infty\)), the AHR and the CDE do not see \(r\); only the windowed margHR(40) moves. With a harmed \(H^*\) the region’s profile starts at its CDE, above 1, while the treated \(H^*\) patients fail, crosses 1 once they are spent and settles near \(b\); the slower clock keeps the 40-month window in the harm phase and moves the region’s margHR(40) toward the null. A regional prognostic effect, a harmed subgroup and a finite window are needed together.

The first-order and events forms. Setting every imbalance to zero gives \[ \operatorname{expit}(\beta^*_{\mathcal S}) \approx (1 - \omega_{\mathcal S})\frac{b}{1+b} + \omega_{\mathcal S}\frac{h}{1+h}, \] \(\omega_{\mathcal S}\) the share of the set’s expected events in the window carried by \(H^*\), with a closed form through the event probability \(\pi(\theta) = 1 - \tfrac{1}{t_e}\int_{t_a - t_e}^{t_a}\exp\{-c\,w^{1/\tau}\}\,dw\), \(c = e^{\theta - \mu/\tau}\). It fails for a harmed \(H^*\), whose treated patients are used up early. Exactly, the score equation is \(D_1/(D_1 + D_0) = \langle\operatorname{expit}(\beta^* + \delta)\rangle_N\), \(D_z\) the arms’ event probabilities and \(\langle\cdot\rangle_N\) the events-weighted average over the window; expanded about \(\bar\delta = \langle\delta\rangle_N\), \[ \beta^* \approx \log\frac{D_1}{D_0} - \bar\delta - \tfrac12(1 - 2\bar P)\,\mathrm{Var}_N(\delta), \qquad \bar P = \frac{D_1}{D_1 + D_0}: \] the marginal hazard ratio is the ratio of the arms’ event probabilities divided by the geometric-mean ratio of the arms’ numbers at risk at the event times.

The design layer. For a trial of \(n\) patients, 1:1, with \(n_{\mathcal S} \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n, \pi_{\mathcal S})\) in \(\mathcal S\) and \(i_1 = \int r(1 - r)\,dN\) the information per patient, \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Var}(\hat\beta_{\mathcal S}) &\approx \frac{1}{i_1}\,\mathrm E\Bigl[\frac{1}{n_{\mathcal S}}\Bigr] && \text{(model)},\\ &\approx \frac{\Sigma}{i_1^2}\,\mathrm E\Bigl[\frac{1}{n_{\mathcal S}}\Bigr] && \text{(robust)},\\ \mathrm E\Bigl[\frac{1}{n_{\mathcal S}}\Bigr] &\approx \frac{1}{n\pi_{\mathcal S}}\Bigl\{1 + \frac{1 - \pi_{\mathcal S}}{n\pi_{\mathcal S}}\Bigr\}, \end{aligned} \] \(\Sigma\) the variance of the Lin–Wei influence. Under a common proportional-hazards model the correlation of nested estimates is the square root of the information share, \(\rho = \mathrm{Corr}(\hat\beta_{\text{all}}, \hat\beta_R) = \sqrt{I_R/I_{\text{all}}}\); under misspecification the layer uses the exact covariance of the two influences. With \(\mu_{\mathcal S} = \beta^*_{\mathcal S}\), \(\sigma_{\mathcal S}\) the robust SD, \(\tilde\sigma_{\text{all}}\) the model SE and \(z = 1.96\), \[ \begin{aligned} P(\text{ITT ub} < 1) &= \Phi(z_A), & z_A &= \frac{-z\tilde\sigma_{\text{all}} - \mu_{\text{all}}}{\sigma_{\text{all}}};\\ P(\text{region ITT} > 1) &= \Phi(-z_B), & z_B &= \frac{-\mu_R}{\sigma_R};\\ P(\text{trigger}) &= \Phi_2(z_A, -z_B; -\rho_{\text{all},R}), \end{aligned} \] and the oracle joint is the trivariate \(\Phi_3(z_A, -z_B, z_C; \mathbf R)\) with \(z_C = -\mu_{G^*}/\sigma_{G^*}\), \(\mathbf R\) the correlation matrix of \((\hat\beta_{\text{all}}, -\hat\beta_R, \hat\beta_{G^*})\) (ahr_design()).

Per-patient entry. With entry_delay, patient \(i\) enters at \(a_i + E\), \(E \sim U(0, t_e)\); each patient carries their own entry factor \(H_{w,i}(u)\), and the arm functions of the score become the entry-weighted sums \(A_{H}(u) = |\mathcal S|^{-1}\sum_{\mathcal S} H_{w,i}(u)\,e^{-u e^{\theta_{1,i}}}\) (and likewise for the control arm and the event densities), with quadrature breaks at each entry group’s kinks. For a set inside a region delayed by \(a\), the limit equals the undelayed limit at horizon \(t_a - a\): a later-enrolling region is a region analysed earlier. With no delay every \(H_{w,i}\) is the common \(H_w\) and the layer is the one above.
